items.title: filer: harden TUS session authorization against cross-prefix access
items.body:
Follow-up hardening for the filer TUS resumable-upload handler when `jwt.filer_signing` uses `allowed_prefixes` for tenant isolation.

Scope-checking HEAD/PATCH/DELETE against the session's stored `TargetPath` closed the direct cross-prefix write, but the surrounding authorization still had gaps: an empty scoped-path list authorized on signature alone, the uploads route accepted aliased ids, and completion re-read chunks without re-checking the session it was authorized for.

Three changes, each in its own commit:

- **Fail closed on a missing resource path.** Split the filer JWT check into `authenticateFilerJwt` (signature + method) and `authorizeFilerJwtPaths` (resource scope). A prefix-restricted token with no resolved path is now denied instead of authorized. The TUS handler authenticates first, reads and validates the session once, authorizes the stored `TargetPath`, then operates on that single pinned snapshot. `readTusSessionInfo` rejects a session whose id, target or size is unusable.

- **Reject non-canonical upload ids.** The route took the first path component as the id, so a trailing path aliased one session under several URLs. The id must now be a canonical UUID, the only form the server mints, at routing and when reading metadata.

- **Revalidate before completion.** Before landing the final entry, confirm the session still exists and its target, size and creation time match the authorized snapshot, so a PATCH finishing after a concurrent DELETE or metadata replacement cannot write to an unauthorized path.

Tests drive the full handler: cross-prefix HEAD/PATCH/DELETE denied with the victim session preserved, matching-prefix allowed, fail-closed on an empty scope, aliased/invalid metadata resolved to not-found, and pinned-session revalidation on delete/replace. `go test ./weed/server` and `go test -race ./weed/server -run TestFilerServer_'(checkJwtAuthorization|tusHandler|refreshTusSessionChunks)'` pass.

items.title: mount: invalidate hot directory listings by section
items.body:
Addresses the analysis in #10708: browsing a directory while another client keeps writing into it drives sustained CPU on the mount.

The per-event cache maintenance was already incremental, but the hot-directory heuristic dropped the whole cached listing once a directory saw 64 changes within 2s and flipped it to read-through. With a continuous writer that cycles forever: wipe, full direct listing, full rebuild, wipe again, with every sibling lookup in between going to the filer as its own LookupEntry call. The cost of one invalidation was the size of the directory, not the size of the change.

This replaces the whole-directory drop with sectioned invalidation. When a listing is built, every 1024th name becomes a section boundary, so the directory is tiled into contiguous name ranges. A burst of foreign changes now invalidates only the section it lands in. Nothing is wiped: the section's entries keep serving and events keep applying; invalidation just means the next readdir re-lists that one range from the filer at a snapshot and reconciles it through the existing version gate, so the listing can never roll back a newer applied event, and pinned local-only entries (deferred creates) survive. Lookups for names in an invalidated section read through to the filer until the range is re-validated. A section that outgrows twice its target size is re-split during its refresh.

Two behavior refinements fall out of the same change: the mount's own writes no longer invalidate its cache (they are ground truth for it, and the old counter tripping on local bursts is what forced the deferred-create fallback in lookupEntry), and a small directory degenerates to a single section, so it keeps today's invalidation trigger but pays one range listing instead of a wipe-and-rebuild cycle.

This applies to the FUSE mount and the Windows mount alike; Windows just makes it more visible because Explorer re-stats on every change notification. For the reported 30,000-file folder note that the directory also exceeds the default -cacheDirMaxEntries=10000 and is never cached at all; raising that flag is needed there for any of this to engage.

  - Added section-based directory metadata caching for targeted refreshes.
  - Automatically refreshes stale listing sections while browsing, including paginated updates.
  - Preserves local changes and pinned entries during cache reconciliation.
  - Splits oversized sections to maintain efficient listing performance.

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Limits invalidation to affected sections instead of entire directories.
  - Prevents stale metadata from unnecessarily forcing full read-through behavior.
  - Falls back to direct directory listing when a section cannot be refreshed safely.

items.title: mount: version open file handles by filer log position
items.body:
Fixes #10394

A metadata event refreshing an open handle re-looked the path up; a transient failure left the handle permanently pinned to its old entry, since the subscription cursor had already advanced. The first attempt to fix this (#10395) applied the event's entry directly, and review then found a sequence of rollback races: each fix manufactured an ordering signal out of band from the state it protected — a delivered-event cursor, a pre-RPC ping, a stable-read retry — and each approximation had a window the next reproduction lived in. This redoes the fix on a single invariant instead: the filer log position is the version of any filer state, and the version travels with the value.

Filer side, lookup and remote-cache responses now carry a log timestamp stamped before the serving read — events are logged after their store write on that clock, so everything at or below the stamp is provably reflected in the returned entry. Mutation acks already carry it in their returned event, and the mount's local store pairs each read with a version cursor advanced under the same lock as the store write.

Mount side, every handle records the version its entry reflects, and one rule replaces the per-site reasoning: state at or below the handle's version must not be installed. Invalidations apply the event's own entry with the event's version — no lookup, so no transient-failure window — except under a cached parent, where the store entry is the ordered merge of the event and anything applied since. Opens version fresh handles from the lookup response; flushes, truncates, and remote-cache downloads version from their acks. Directory builds version the completed directory at the listing snapshot and re-invalidate buffered events at that version.

The test suite replays every race found in the previous attempt as a deterministic reproduction against a fake filer: rollback of a newer local flush in queued, cached, and read-through configurations; stale leftovers under uncached parents; the build window including abort; handles opened after an event was queued; events landing mid-lookup; and undelivered events at remote-cache time across a filer failover.

Known residuals, inherent to per-filer clocks: multi-filer clock skew can make a fence conservatively skip one event until the next arrives, and eventless acks from pre-upgrade filers leave the handle unversioned, degrading to today's behavior. The server-side copy path installs its result unversioned and converges when the copy's own committed event is delivered.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Prevented open file handles and cached entries from being overwritten or rolled back by older metadata events by fencing refreshes with filer log/version timestamps (including save/update acknowledgements, renames/deletes, queued notifications, and remote-entry downloads).
  * Improved metadata cache version tracking so invalidations and buffered directory-build events are applied consistently.
  * Added filer response log-position timestamps to better support consistent acknowledgement handling.
* **Tests**
  * Expanded coverage for versioned invalidation, rollback fencing, buffering/directory build behavior, concurrent open races, and remote-cache failover scenarios.

items.title: filer postgres2 (and postgres) backend: DROP TABLE must use IF EXISTS to avoid 42P01 panic crash-loop on concurrent bucket deletions
items.body:
## Summary

When a bucket is deleted, all filer replicas receive the deletion event simultaneously. The first replica to run `DROP TABLE "pvc-<uuid>"` succeeds. All other replicas hit **postgres error 42P01 (undefined_table)** because the table is already gone. The filer does **not** handle 42P01 — it panics, restarts, and immediately re-attempts the same `DROP TABLE` → crash-loop.

The fix is a one-line change in two files: `drop table "%s"` → `drop table if exists "%s"`.

## Affected code

**`weed/filer/postgres2/postgres2_store.go`**

```go
// Current (triggers 42P01 on concurrent DELETE):
DropTableSqlTemplate: `drop table "%s"`,

// Fix:
DropTableSqlTemplate: `drop table if exists "%s"`,
```

**`weed/filer/postgres/postgres_store.go`** — identical issue, same fix.

Both files carry the same `DropTableSqlTemplate` field with bare `DROP TABLE`. Verified on master as of 2026-06-29.

## Repro steps

1. Deploy seaweedfs with **3+ filer replicas** and the **postgres2** filer backend (or postgres).
2. Create an S3 bucket — this creates a matching postgres table (e.g. `"pvc-abc123"`).
3. Delete the bucket via the S3 API.
4. All 3 filers receive the `OnBucketDeletion` event simultaneously.
5. Filer-0 runs `DROP TABLE "pvc-abc123"` — succeeds.
6. Filer-1 runs `DROP TABLE "pvc-abc123"` → postgres error `ERROR: table "pvc-abc123" does not exist (SQLSTATE 42P01)`.
7. Filer-1 panics and restarts.
8. On restart, filer-1 has the same pending DROP in its startup queue → panics again → crash-loop.

**Observed in production**: with 3 filer replicas, a single bucket deletion generated a crash-loop lasting ~9 minutes across all 3 filers, taking the S3 gateway offline.

## Call path (postgres2)

```
S3 DeleteBucket
  → filer.OnBucketDeletion(bucket)      [filer.go]
      → store.DeleteFolderChildren(ctx, bucket)
          → postgres2Store.deleteTable(ctx, bucket)
              → db.ExecContext(ctx, `drop table "pvc-abc123"`)
                  ← 42P01 if table already gone
              ← error propagated
          ← error propagated → panic
```

Note: `OnBucketDeletion` in some paths swallows the error, but `DeleteFolderChildren` does not — the panic originates there.

## Fix

```diff
// weed/filer/postgres2/postgres2_store.go
-DropTableSqlTemplate: `drop table "%s"`,
+DropTableSqlTemplate: `drop table if exists "%s"`,

// weed/filer/postgres/postgres_store.go
-DropTableSqlTemplate: `drop table "%s"`,
+DropTableSqlTemplate: `drop table if exists "%s"`,
```

`DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` is standard SQL and is supported by all postgres versions that seaweedfs targets.

## Environment

- seaweedfs: 4.37 (latest as of 2026-06-29), confirmed present in master
- Filer backend: postgres2 (CNPG-managed PostgreSQL 17.4)
- Filer replicas: 3
- Trigger: concurrent `OnBucketDeletion` across 3 replicas for the same bucket

## Workaround

Until this is fixed upstream, a periodic reconciler can be run against the postgres database that:
1. Finds `pvc-*` bucket entries in `filemeta` at `directory='/buckets'` whose corresponding table is missing → `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` (so the filer's pending DROP can succeed).
2. Finds `pvc-*` postgres tables with no corresponding `filemeta` entry → `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` (orphan cleanup).

This is a band-aid; the correct fix is `IF EXISTS` in the filer code.

items.title: mount: keep directory listings that have been walked through
items.body:
Every enumeration re-read the whole directory out of the local store and decoded
it again, so reopening a folder cost exactly what opening it did. That is most of
what a readdir spends. This is the item left open at the end of #10616.

A walk that covers a directory from its first child to its last now leaves the
decoded entries behind, and the next walk pages through them in memory.

```
                    time      bytes       allocations
    first walk    198.1ms   190.3 MiB   2.05M
    reopened       76.2ms    21.4 MiB   1.00M
                   -62%       -89%       -51%
```

200k-entry directory, medians of 8 samples in one run. What remains on the warm
path is the readdir's own per-entry work — building each child's path, resolving
its inode, filling the attribute block — not the listing.

**Only a complete walk is cached.** Nothing is published from a walk that stopped
early or started partway in, so `ls | head` on a huge directory does not pay for
the rest of it. The build is carried across pages and only published when the
store runs out without the caller having stopped it — the distinction that
matters, because a caller whose buffer filled has also produced a short page.

**Invalidation is not a timer.** The cache holds only what the meta cache holds,
so it is void whenever that is. Every write to the local store now goes through
one of four wrappers, each dropping the directory it touched under the same lock
that made the write; reaching past them for a write would leave a listing stale,
and there is a comment saying so. A rebuild drops the listing at begin and at
complete. A walk publishes only if its build is still the live one for that
directory, so a write landing halfway through cannot leave a stale listing
behind. A subscription gap drops everything, since the mount cannot know what it
missed.

**Expiry is the one thing that changes with no write at all**, so it is applied
when serving rather than invalidated for. A cached listing must not go stale
just because a child aged out while it sat there, and a TTL-driven invalidation
would be guesswork. Serving also has to step over expired children the way the
store does — counting them against the limit and advancing the cursor past them
— or pagination diverges between a hit and a miss. That is the same trap as the
truncation bug in #10624.

**Only chunkless listings are cached or served.** Those are what the readdir path
decodes since #10616, so an entry from the cache can never reach a caller that
wanted chunks.

`-dirListCacheEntries` sizes it, default 200k children (tens of megabytes),
0 disables. Least recently used directories are dropped to stay inside it.

Tests cover the hit, invalidation for each mutation kind (insert, update, delete,
delete-children, rename-in, purge, distrust-all), a partial walk, a mid-directory
listing, a write landing mid-walk, expiry applied on serve without any
invalidation, eviction, and the disabled case.

- **New Features**

  - Added the `-dirListCacheEntries` mount option to configure cache capacity. It defaults to 1,000,000 entries and can be set to zero to disable caching.
  - Cached listings support pagination, expiration filtering, and least-recently-used eviction.

- **Bug Fixes**

items.title: s3: tear down the emptied .versions directory on last-version delete; drain existing residue
items.body:
## What

A versioned `DELETE ?versionId=` of a key's **last** version on the routed write path leaves the key's now-empty `.versions/` directory behind: the owner-filer transaction repoints/clears the latest pointer and deletes the version file, but — unlike the distributed-lock fallback path (`updateLatestVersionAfterDeletion`, which `rm`s the directory) — it has no teardown step.

The residue is not harmless. The key's read path finds the directory, finds no pointer and no versions, and runs the full self-heal — 3×100ms metadata retries, a directory rescan, an `event=surfaced` warning, and a `GetObject: Failed to get latest version` error — on **every GET** until the background `EmptyFolderCleaner` reaches the directory: at least ~2 minutes on its delay queue, and possibly never, since that queue is in-memory (lost on filer restart), bounded (1000 entries, drops on overflow), and gated on the bucket's allow-empty-folders policy. Veeam's lock arbitration (`Lock/{guid}/lock|declare|try`) creates and versionId-deletes lock objects continuously and keeps probing the deleted keys, so these windows are always open in production and the log spam is chronic:

```
W... [versioning-heal] event=surfaced bucket=... key=Veeam/Backup/.../Lock/{guid}/try missing_file= rescanning=.../try.versions
E... GetObject: Failed to get latest version for ...: no version metadata in .versions directory and no regular object found ...
```

Reproduced with one aws-cli cycle (versioned `put-object`, `delete-object --version-id`): the empty directory persists with `Extended: null`, and every subsequent GET emits the pair above.

## Fix

- **Producer** (commit 1): `ObjectMutation` DELETE gains `remove_empty_parent`; the filer removes the parent directory in the same locked transaction after the child delete, best-effort and non-recursive — a concurrent write that lands a new version makes the removal fail rather than being lost with it. `routedDeleteSpecificVersion` sets it on the version-file DELETE, matching the lock-path fallback's contract. Delete markers are unaffected (the marker keeps the directory non-empty).
- **Residue drains** (commit 2): the read-path heal now removes a version-free directory outright (orphan children still block it and fall back to the pointer clear) and logs `event=healed mode=empty_dir_removed`, so pre-existing residue retires on first touch instead of rescanning forever. `s3.versions.audit` gains an `empty` category and `-heal` removes such directories in bulk.

## Verification

- `TestObjectTransactionDeleteRemovesEmptyParent`: last-version delete removes the directory; a remaining child keeps it; idempotent replay still tidies it.
- e2e on a local `weed server`: the lock cycle leaves no `.versions` residue (~1s after delete, no janitor wait) and GETs of the deleted key produce zero `versioning-heal` lines; a manufactured legacy residue dir drains on first GET (`surfaced` once, then `healed mode=empty_dir_removed`, silent afterwards); `s3.versions.audit` reports it as `empty: 1` and `-heal` removes it; an unversioned DELETE (delete marker) leaves the directory intact with no spam.
- `go test ./weed/server/ ./weed/s3api/... ./weed/shell/ ./weed/filer/` all pass.

https://claude.ai/code/session_014mMYAHXZySkCCUfpRFNtSv

  * Enhanced `.versions/` auditing with a new `empty` category, and optional healing to remove empty `.versions/` directories.
* **Bug Fixes**
  * Deleting the last object version now removes the now-empty `.versions/` directory.
  * Stale latest-version pointers are handled more robustly when `.versions/` directories are already empty.
  * DELETE mutations now tolerate “not found” conditions as a no-op.

items.title: s3: give a versioned metadata-only copy its own chunks
items.body:
Fixes #10592.

With versioning enabled, a self-copy that only rewrites metadata cloned the source entry chunk fids and all into a new `.versions/` file. Two live entries then point at one chunk list, and nothing refcounts a plain shared chunk list — deleting either version tombstones the needles the other still needs, and the next vacuum makes the loss permanent. rclone stamps mtime with exactly this copy after every upload, and a `NoncurrentVersionExpiration` rule performs the delete on its own.

Reproduced end to end on a local cluster: after `DELETE ?versionId=` of one version plus a vacuum, the surviving version returns HTTP 200 with a zero-byte body while ListObjectVersions still advertises its full size. No error surfaces at any point.

Two more shapes of the same defect, confirmed the same way:

- A suspended bucket writes the null version at the bare key; when the copy source resolved to a `.versions/` entry (no null entry yet), that entry stays live beside it and they share needles.
- `executeKeyRotation` hands back the source chunks for an SSE-KMS key change on the same "the copy overwrites its source" assumption, which a versioned destination breaks.

## Fix

Take the metadata-only path only where the write replaces the entry it read: the bare key of a bucket without versioning, with no `versionId` pinned on the copy source. Versioned, suspended, and pinned copies fall through to the regular copy path, which gives the destination its own chunks. The key rotation follows the same rule and otherwise reencrypts, which also gives the new version the key it asked for instead of leaving it on the old one.

A versioned metadata touch now costs a real data copy. That matches S3, where every version owns its storage.

## Testing

`TestVersioningSelfCopyMetadataReplaceKeepsChunksIndependent` and `TestSuspendedSelfCopyMetadataReplaceKeepsChunksIndependent` write a chunked object, self-copy it with REPLACE, delete the version the copy read from, then vacuum and re-read the survivor. Both fail on master with `unexpected EOF` from the truncated body and pass with this change. The existing self-copy regression tests and the `test/s3/copying` suite stay green.

## Note on the approach

The issue suggests putting both versions under one `HardLinkId` to borrow the filer's hardlink refcount. That does not hold up: `FilerStoreWrapper.maybeReadHardLink` restores `Attr`, `Chunks`, `Extended`, and `Content` from the blob keyed by the hardlink id, so every linked entry reads back the last writer's metadata — including its version id and ETag. Hard links are a same-inode primitive; S3 versions need their own metadata, so the chunks have to be copied instead.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Fixed self-copy operations with metadata replacement so object content remains intact across versioned and suspended-versioning configurations.
  * Improved handling of large, chunked objects during self-copy and storage cleanup.
  * Prevented unintended sharing of object data when self-copy creates an independent version.
  * Improved encrypted-object copying when creating independent versions.
* **Tests**
  * Added regression coverage for versioning, suspended versioning, pinned versions, and encrypted-object copy scenarios.

items.title: s3: lazy, bounded, entry-free per-bucket caches
items.body:
The S3 gateway warmed two per-bucket caches by listing every bucket at startup, then kept them resident forever: startup was O(buckets) and glog.Fatal'd on a slow filer, and at millions of buckets each gateway pinned gigabytes of duplicated bucket metadata. Three commits:

**Stop warming every bucket's config at startup.** Delete the eager full list in `BucketRegistry.init()`. Both caches already have lazy miss paths, so buckets load from the filer on first access; the metadata subscription refreshes only entries already resident, so each gateway caches its own working set instead of the whole cluster.

**Bound the caches with LRU eviction.** The config cache, bucket registry, and both negative caches were grow-only maps — the config TTL made `Get` miss but never evicted, and the not-found sets grew on every probe of a nonexistent name. All four are now LRUs capped at 65536 entries (hashicorp/golang-lru, already in the module graph).

**Cache parsed config instead of the full filer entry.** Each cached `BucketConfig` retained the whole `filer_pb.Entry` (extended-attribute map plus raw content bytes) alongside the fields parsed from it. Parse everything up front — now also creator identity, tags, encryption, and stored lifecycle XML — and drop the entry. `updateBucketConfig` reads the entry fresh from the filer and diffs the mapped extended attributes against it, so config writes patch against current state instead of a cached copy, and the deep-clone helpers that protected the cached entry go away.

Cost of the trade: one filer round-trip on a cold bucket's first request. Net -592/+296 lines.

items.title: mount: mark windows files archived and ignore a zero timestamp
items.body:
Two defects the WinFsp conformance suite reported, both traced to a specific assertion.

`create_fileattr_test` asserts `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_ARCHIVE` on a new file (`create-test.c:257`). We set no flags at all, so Windows synthesises `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL` — a probe of a fresh file on the mount confirms it reports `Normal`. A regular file now reports `UF_ARCHIVE`, which WinFsp maps to the attribute Windows expects.

`getfileinfo_test` asserts a file created a moment ago has an access time within ten seconds of now (`info-test.c:207`). `Utimens` was writing a zero timestamp through: Windows sends zero for a field it is not setting, my guard only rejected `UTIME_OMIT` and the 1601 epoch, and a stored zero became 1970 in the mount's in-memory atime overlay — which then overrode the entry's real time on every subsequent read. It only showed through an open handle; reading the same file by path took a different route and looked correct, which is why probing a fresh file showed nothing wrong.

Both tests come off `known_failures.txt`. Creation time stays on it: the filer records one, but the raw protocol's `Attr` has no field for it outside darwin, so ctime still stands in.

items.title: s3: surface transient store errors during multipart resume/copy instead of masking them
items.body:
Fixes #10194.

## Problem

The Docker Registry v3 S3 driver uploads a blob by starting an S3 multipart upload for `_uploads/<uuid>/data`, resuming it on each PATCH/PUT via `ListMultipartUploads(prefix=key)` (with a `Stat` fallback), and committing with a server-side copy (`Move`). With a filer backed by an external metadata store (MariaDB) and concurrent uploads (skopeo copies layers in parallel even for a sequential push), a transient store error during those calls was masked as a terminal, non-retryable response:

- `listMultipartUploads` returned `200` with an empty list on any `s3a.list` error. The driver reads that as "no in-progress upload" → `PathNotFoundError` → `500 error resolving upload: Path not found: .../data`.
- `listObjectParts` returned `NoSuchUpload` on a list error → same effect on resume.
- CopyObject source resolution returned `InvalidArgument: Copy Source must mention the source bucket and key` on *any* lookup error, transient ones included → the commit `Move` fails with a non-retryable `400`.

Since these are 4xx / false-success, clients don't retry, so an intermittent metadata-store blip fails the whole image push.

## Fix

Surface the store error as a retryable `ErrInternalError` (5xx) in all three spots. A genuinely missing, invalid, or directory copy source keeps its existing client error.

## Verification

Reproduced with real `registry:3.0.0` + `skopeo/1.13.3` → `weed server -s3 -filer` on a MariaDB filer store, forcing transient list errors by capping MariaDB connections under concurrent copies.

- Before: registry logs `Path not found` and `Copy Source must mention the source bucket and key`; pushes fail with `500`.
- After: none of either; the same failures surface as retryable `InternalError: ... please try again`, so brief blips are retried and the push completes.

`go test ./weed/s3api/` passes.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Improved multipart upload listing and part listing to return the correct “upload not found”/empty results when uploads are missing.
  * Updated multipart abort behavior to distinguish genuine “no such upload” from unexpected store failures.
  * Refined CopyObject/CopyObjectPart behavior to return more accurate errors when the copy source is nil, a directory, a delete-marker, has an invalid version, is unavailable, or encounters internal issues.
  * Added validation so invalid part IDs fail with the proper error response.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

items.title: operation: re-assign chunk upload when replica volume is full
items.body:
## Problem

`UploadReaderInChunks` uploads each chunk with `uploader.UploadData`, which bottoms out in `retriedUploadData` — three attempts against the same URL, no reassignment. So one bad volume fails the whole object: a replica at capacity answers every attempt with `Volume Size 34361499680 Exceeded 34359738368`, and a backup job that keeps landing on it fails for hours waiting on GC.

The non-chunked path does not have this problem. `uploadWithRetryData` wraps `retriedUploadData` in `RetryOnError(shouldReassignUpload, ...)`, which asks the filer for a fresh volume on any 5xx — `TestUploadWithRetryDataReassignsOnVolumeSizeExceeded` pins exactly this error string. Chunked uploads just never got wired to it.

## Fix

Wrap the chunk upload in a reassignment loop gated on the same `shouldReassignUpload` the non-chunked path uses. It keys off the status the volume server returned rather than matching message text, so it also recovers from a lost replica peer (`failed to write to replicas`) and an unreachable target, while leaving a 4xx alone — a second volume would reject that identically. Bounded at `chunkAssignAttempts` (3) volumes per chunk.

The single attempt moves into `uploadChunk` so the loop reads cleanly over both the fan-out and the cipher relay path.

## What this does and does not guarantee

The master drops a volume from `writables` when its **configured** `volumeSizeLimit` is reached, via `VolumeLayout.RecordAssign` eagerly or `SetVolumeCapacityFull` off the heartbeat. Nothing marks a volume full at `MaxPossibleVolumeSize`, and the volume server does not flip it read-only either.

So in the configuration that produces the error above — `volumeSizeLimitMB` set past the 32 GiB 4-byte-offset ceiling — the master still considers the volume writable, and `weightedPick` can hand back the same one. Reassignment makes the upload *likely* to recover rather than certain to; with a single writable volume in the layout it will not recover at all.

That is worth fixing separately (clamping `volumeSizeLimitMB` to `MaxPossibleVolumeSize` at master startup would turn this into a config error instead of a runtime one). Retrying somewhere else is the right client-side reflex regardless, and it is what the non-chunked path already does.

## Reproduction

Fill a replica volume to `MaxPossibleVolumeSize`. Any multi-replica chunked upload assigned to it fails with:

```
chunked upload failed: upload chunk: unmarshalled error ... Volume Size 34361499680 Exceeded 34359738368
```

With this change the chunk is offered to a different volume and succeeds.

## Rollback

`ReplicatedWrite` commits the needle locally before it replicates, so a 5xx can leave a copy behind on the volume the chunk then walks away from. Nothing will reference that fid, and an unreferenced needle is not garbage vacuum can find. `uploadChunkToHolders` rolls back only the holders that reported success — it misses the one whose write landed but whose response did not — and the relay path had none at all, so the loop deletes the abandoned fid from every holder of that assignment. That runs on every failed attempt, including the one that exhausts the budget: giving up is exactly when nothing else will ever name that fid, since the caller only gets back the chunks that succeeded.

## Retry budget

`retriedUploadData` already retries a chunk three times against the same URL, so wrapping it in three assignments would have made nine POSTs per chunk, unbounded by time — the S3 handler passes `context.Background()` so a chunk survives client disconnect, which also means no deadline cuts the loop short. The relay path is capped at one upload call per assignment (the loop retries everything it would, on a better target), keeping the budget at three. That bounds `retriedUploadData` only — `doUploadData` still reissues once on a connection reset with a rewound body, which is a transport stutter inside a single call rather than another attempt at the volume, so a reset-heavy path can still cost two round trips per assignment. The fan-out path keeps its inner retries: absorbing a blip on one holder beats cancelling the rest and re-uploading the chunk. The loop also stops once another chunk has already failed the object.

## Tests

`...ReassignsOnFullVolume`, `...DoesNotReassignOnClientError` and `...BoundsReassignment` cover the three outcomes the gate decides, and check that each attempt carries its own assignment JWT. `...ReassignsAcrossHolders` drives the replica fan-out with real servers and asserts the abandoned fid is rolled back from both holders while the reassigned volume keeps its copy. `...DoesNotMultiplyRelayAttempts` pins both the per-assignment upload budget and that every abandoned fid — the last one included — is rolled back.

items.title: fix(mount): keep a deferred local create from vanishing when its dir is rebuilt
items.body:
`wfs.Create` defers the filer create to Flush and inserts a local-only placeholder into the metaCache (`dirtyMetadata=true`), so a just-created file exists locally before the filer has it. When the parent directory falls out of cache (hot-dir read-through, idle evict) and is rebuilt, `EnsureVisited` wipes the store and refills from a filer listing that does not yet include the un-flushed create, then `markCachedFn` publishes the directory authoritatively cached without it. `lookupEntry` then returns an authoritative ENOENT and `ReadDir` returns nothing — the file disappears from the mount although the client created it. Under concurrent read+write churn on one directory this surfaces as the `ConcurrentReadWrite` integration flake.

This extends the apply-loop serialization work (the external evict/Forget/copy-range/retry wipes were already routed through it) to the rebuild's own wipe+refill, which still discarded local-only entries the filer snapshot had not caught up to.

Preserve children the mount flags as local-only — an open dirty handle or a pending async flush, the same signal `lookupEntry` already trusts over a filer `ErrNotFound` — across the rebuild's wipe instead of blind-deleting them. Unpinned stale children are still dropped so a rebuild cannot resurrect a deleted entry.

`TestEnsureVisitedPreservesLocalOnlyEntry` reproduces the loss (fails without the fix); `TestEnsureVisitedDropsUnpinnedStaleEntry` guards the selectivity. `./weed/mount/...` passes, including under `-race`.

items.title: preserve Content-Encoding for remote-mounted objects
items.body:
Fixes #10339.

A RemoteEntry now records the remote object's Content-Encoding, and every path that materializes a local entry from remote metadata (lazy fetch, lazy listing, remote.mount, remote.meta.sync, remote.cache) stamps it into the entry extended attributes, the same place a native S3 upload stores it. HTTP and S3 HeadObject/GetObject then return the header with no read-path changes.

The proto field is optional so presence is explicit: GCS and Azure report the encoding on listing and stat, and any stat is authoritative, so an encoding removed on the remote clears the stamped header on the next sync. S3 listings do not carry encodings, so they leave the field unset and never touch a known value; the sync triggers only treat a reported encoding as a change. For list-backed S3 mounts, remote.meta.sync -statFiles stats each new or changed file whose listing left the encoding unreported and persists the result, so repeat runs only stat what changed.

The reverse direction is covered too: filer.remote.sync and remote.copy.local set Content-Encoding on the uploaded GCS/S3/Azure object, and a metadata-only change (same content) reaches the remote header everywhere — GCS patches contentEncoding alongside custom metadata, Azure reissues the blob's HTTP headers with the rest carried over, and S3 reissues the object as an in-place copy with replaced metadata (beyond the 5 GiB copy limit the change is logged and applies on the next content write).

One related GCS fix: reads now request the stored bytes (ReadCompressed). GCS decompressive transcoding of gzip-encoded objects ignores range requests and returns sizes that disagree with the tracked RemoteSize, so chunked reads of such objects would fail.

For an existing mount, `remote.meta.sync` or `remote.cache` picks up the encoding on its next run against a GCS or Azure remote; on S3 remotes use `remote.meta.sync -statFiles` or rely on per-object stats and rewrites.

items.title: s3: paginate ListBuckets and serve it from a bucket owner index
items.body:
ListBuckets listed all of /buckets with MaxInt32, buffered every entry into one slice, ran a per-bucket permission check, and serialized one giant XML body. With very large bucket counts that is slow and eventually OOMs, and it answers a per-caller question by scanning the global namespace.

**Pagination.** The handler now pages through the filer listing and caps each response at 10000 buckets like AWS, honoring `max-buckets`, `prefix`, and an opaque keyset `continuation-token` (echoed back as `ContinuationToken` when the listing is truncated). It never buffers the full bucket set.

**Owner index.** Each bucket is indexed under its owner at `/buckets/.system/owners/<owner>/<bucket>` as a zero-length entry whose Crtime mirrors the bucket's creation time. The bucket handlers write the index synchronously so ListBuckets stays read-your-writes; the existing /buckets metadata subscription reconciles changes made elsewhere (weed shell, other gateways, direct filer operations, ownership claims); and a startup backfill indexes pre-existing buckets, then writes a ready marker. Until the marker exists, reads keep the paged scan, so upgrades need no migration step. Owner names are path-escaped so no identity name can traverse out of the index.

Once ready, a non-admin identity's ListBuckets costs O(its own buckets): owned buckets come straight from the index, merged with any buckets its actions name explicitly (`List:bucket`, `Admin:bucket`), each still checked through the normal permission path. Admins, identities with a bare `List` grant, and wildcard action patterns keep the paged scan since their visible set can't be enumerated.

One behavior change: identities authorized through IAM policies (JWT/STS/attached policies) now see their owned buckets, matching AWS where ListBuckets returns only the caller's buckets; previously any bucket a policy granted `s3:ListBucket` on appeared in the listing.

Also keeps `.system` out of every bucket surface: dot-prefixed names no longer resolve as buckets and the shell bucket listing skips them.

Covered by unit tests (arg parsing, token round-trip, owner escaping, classifier, merge/truncation) and an integration test that boots a mini cluster with four identities and verifies pagination on both paths, grant visibility, index contents on the filer, delete, and that `.system` is unreachable.

items.title: Cut per-subscriber replay decode and widen replay concurrency
items.body:
## What

**Filter metadata events before unmarshaling them per subscriber.** Every subscriber unmarshaled every log entry into a full event just to run the path filter, and entries carry complete chunk lists — so a fleet of path-filtered subscribers (CSI mounts watching their own volume paths) spends almost all replay CPU materializing events it then discards: with 150 per-path subscribers, ~149 of every 150 decodes were wasted. A shallow wire scan now extracts just the directory, entry names and rename destination into a skeleton event and feeds the existing matcher, so the filter decision costs a few small allocations instead of materializing chunk lists. Anything surprising in the payload (malformed bytes, merged duplicate message fields) falls back to the full decode, broad subscribers without path filters skip the scan entirely, and the unsynced-events heartbeat keeps firing for skipped entries so client cursors still advance. Equivalence between the skeleton match and the full-decode match is covered across create/update/delete/rename shapes and filter kinds.

**Raise the legacy replay cap from 16 to 64.** The cap was sized when every replay pinned a private 8MB chunk reader per source filer; replays now share decoded chunks, so the old value needlessly serializes subscriber catch-up.

**Weight concurrent chunk loads by size.** The flat eight-load gate admitted eight tiny chunks as reluctantly as eight full 8MB ones. Each load now charges its chunk size against a 128MB in-flight budget: small chunks decode wide open, full-size ones still serialize enough to cap the transient fetch+decode peak, and oversized weights clamp to the budget so they can always acquire.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Performance Improvements**
  * Raised concurrency cap for persisted-log replay and added size-aware load throttling to improve chunk-loading throughput and reduce contention.

* **New Features**
  * Added lightweight metadata-event skeleton scanning to prefilter and skip full decoding for non-matching subscriptions, lowering latency for path-filtered subscribers.
  * Shared unsynced-event tracking across replay and delivery to unify heartbeat/unsynced behavior.

* **Tests**
  * New and extended tests and benchmarks covering cache behavior, large-load handling, skeleton scanning, and subscription prefiltering.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Benchmark

Controlled replay wave, two passes per side: write an identical dataset (63.6K appends, ~150 path-filtered directories, no subscribers attached), then have 150 subscribers replay the whole history at once with no churn.

|  | master, pass 1 / 2 | this PR, pass 1 / 2 |
|---|---|---|
| filer CPU for the wave | 27m49s / 30m11s, cut off incomplete at the 5-minute cap | 1m43s / 1m18s |
| wall time to drain | over 302s / 301s, ~13% of events undelivered | 46s / 35s |
| events delivered | 58.6K / 60.8K (truncated) | 67.3K / 67.3K (complete) |
| live heap mid-wave | 670MB | 651MB |

About 20x less CPU for the same replay work, matching the per-entry microbenchmark, with the same cache-dominated live heap. The baseline burns six cores for five minutes and still does not finish; the PR drains the same wave in well under a minute.

items.title: shell: multi-target fs.mergeVolumes and volume.mark -readonlyCanDelete
items.body:
Fixes #10688.

Two ways to reclaim volume slots stuck around 50% usage:

`fs.mergeVolumes -fromVolumeId=112 -toVolumeId=111,107` accepts a comma-separated target list now. Each chunk is routed to the target with the most remaining capacity, so a volume that fits into no single target can still be cleared. A single target, or no explicit ids, behaves as before. Without `-fromVolumeId`, the list restricts the heuristic planner's target candidates.

`volume.mark -readonlyCanDelete` (with `-node`/`-volumeId` or `-collection`) marks a volume so new writes are rejected but deletes still land. A volume holding expiring data then drains over time until it can be vacuumed away or merged into other volumes. The state persists to `.vif` and survives restarts; the master sees the volume as read-only so it assigns no new writes; `-writable` clears it. On the wire this is a new `can_delete` field on `VolumeMarkReadonlyRequest`, mirrored in the Rust volume server.

items.title: fix(volume [rust]): compare live compaction_revision instead of stale last_compact_revision
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?
last_compact_revision() returns a bookkeeping field recorded just before a compaction starts (for makeup-diff catch-up), intentionally left behind the live super_block.compaction_revision afterward. Go's reference implementation compares against the live v.CompactionRevision in both CopyFile's precondition check and the heartbeat's VolumeInformationMessage. Using the stale field in either spot causes permanent, deterministic failures ("volume N is compacted") on any volume that has ever been compacted even once, and corrupts the master's cluster-wide view of every such volume's compaction state.

grpc_server.rs — copy_file's precondition check: compare against v.super_block.compaction_revision instead — the live, current value — matching what Go's reference implementation does (v.CompactionRevision, the embedded SuperBlock field).
heartbeat.rs — the VolumeInformationMessage sent to the master: same fix: compact_revision now reports vol.super_block.compaction_revision instead of the stale vol.last_compact_revision()

items.title: s3: rescan .versions when the cached latest pointer is missing on a list
items.body:
Companion to the RECOMPUTE_LATEST notify fix, on the read side.

ListObjectsV2 (what `mc du` / `mc ls` use) resolves a versioned object's current version from the latest-version pointer cached on the `.versions` directory entry, for a single-scan listing. When that pointer is absent on the filer serving the list - e.g. a multi-filer cluster where the pointer was written on the key's owner filer and hasn't converged - `getLatestVersionEntryFromDirectoryEntry` returned an error and the object was silently dropped from the listing, so the bucket looked far smaller than it is.

Fall back to a read-only rescan of `.versions/` to pick the newest version when the cached pointer is missing. The version files replicate even when the pointer doesn't, so the rescan resolves the current version locally. This is the listing-side counterpart to the read path's `recoverLatestVersionWithoutPointer`; the pagination/select loop is factored into a shared `scanLatestVersionEntry`.

Read-only on purpose: a list can touch many objects, so it does not persist a pointer (no write amplification). Overhead is zero when the pointer is present (fast path unchanged) and ~one local `.versions/` list per pointer-missing object otherwise.

Verified on a 3-filer cluster: source 122 objects, versioned bucket `mc du` 122/168 MiB on all endpoints (was 32/4 MiB). s3api unit tests pass; single-filer versioning tests unaffected.

items.title: s3: route non-conditional suspended DELETE off the DLM
items.body:
Closes the suspended-versioning race: now that suspended PUT routes on the object key (per-path entry lock), a suspended DELETE left on the distributed lock wouldn't serialize against it — the two locks are independent. This routes suspended DELETE on the object key too.

A suspended DELETE removes the null version (the **main object** entry) and adds a delete marker. `FinalizeVersionedWrite` gains an optional `delete_path` it deletes under the same object-key lock before flipping the pointer, so "delete null + add marker" is one atomic step on the owner. `createDeleteMarker` threads it through (empty for the versioning-enabled marker path; the null path for suspended).

Scope: routed only when there's **no `If-Match`** — that condition targets the main object, not the `.versions` pointer the op evaluates, so a conditional suspended delete stays on the lock path. Object-lock can't apply (it requires versioning enabled, never suspended).

Stacked on the routing series + the object-lock-gate PR; merge after them.

items.title: ObjectTransaction: filer-side forwarding via route_key
items.body:
The route-by-key gateway resolves an object's owner filer from a consistent-hash ring and sends each `ObjectTransaction` straight to it. The owner's per-path lock is what serializes concurrent writes to the same key — but only if the request actually lands on the owner. When the gateway's ring view lags a membership change, it can route to a filer that no longer owns the key, and that filer would lock and apply locally, splitting the serialization point.

This closes that gap with filer-side forwarding, the same mechanism the distributed lock already relies on:

- `ObjectTransactionRequest` gains `route_key` (the ring key) and `is_moved`.
- A filer that receives a transaction whose `route_key` it does not own forwards the whole transaction to the ring owner. The forward sets `is_moved`, which the receiver honors by applying locally instead of forwarding again — bounding it to one hop so two filers that briefly disagree on the owner cannot loop. Mirrors `DistributedLock`'s `movedTo`/`IsMoved` handling.
- The gateway stamps `route_key` on every routed builder (non-versioned PUT/DELETE, versioned finalize, version-specific and null-version deletes, mkfile, metadata self-copy, bucket config) through one `objectRouteKey` helper. The filer's `LockRing` and the gateway's `LockClient` ring are the same `lock_manager.HashRing`, so they resolve the same owner; forwarding only corrects a stale gateway view.

With forwarding in place, route-by-key is self-sufficient: a misrouted transaction still serializes on the true owner's lock rather than needing the distributed-lock fallback to cover the miss.

items.title: heartbeat: send only the volumes that changed
items.body:
The step where the cost in #10603 actually goes away. Builds on #10619 and #10627.

A volume server has been resending its whole volume list every 5 seconds because that list was the only way the master could notice a volume that vanished without a delta. The digest now gives that guarantee, so the list can stop.

```
2000 volumes on the server
  full list heartbeat:     30004 bytes (2000 volumes)
  steady-state heartbeat:    131 bytes (0 changed)
```

At the 550k-volume scale in #10603 that is 28MB and ~229MB of master allocation per server every 5 seconds becoming a few hundred bytes, plus whatever genuinely moved. The read-only and tiered volumes that make up most of that cluster never appear at all.

## Wire

```proto
message Heartbeat {
  repeated VolumeInformationMessage changed_volumes = 28;
}
message HeartbeatResponse {
  bool volume_digest_supported = 9;
}
```

A partial list cannot travel in `volumes`: a master that did not understand it would read the absences as deletions and drop the lot. So changes get their own field, and are sent only once the master has said it compares digests — a server reaching an older master, or reconnecting to one, is back to full lists straight away with no deployment ordering to get right.

## Two things that would have been very bad

**`has_no_volumes` must come from a full list alone.** It was derived from the outgoing message; in delta mode a heartbeat with nothing to report carries nothing, which would have read as *this server holds no volumes* and dropped every volume on it. It is now false unless a full list is being sent, and `TestQuietHeartbeatDoesNotLookLikeAnEmptyServer` fails against the earlier version.

**The digest covers everything held, not what was sent.** Otherwise a master that correctly applied the changes could never confirm it was current.

## Rust

Mirrored, with a hazard the Go side does not have: mount and unmount deltas there are derived by diffing successive heartbeats against the last `volumes` list, so a partial list would have reported every volume it left out as unmounted. Collecting now returns the full set alongside the message, and all four sites that diff use that rather than what went on the wire.

## Reporting state

Per connection, so a reconnect or a different master starts from the full list. Keyed by (disk, volume) rather than volume id, since an id mounted on two disks would otherwise leave one copy's changes untold. A volume that goes away is forgotten, so one that comes back is reported again.

Its zero value means nothing has been told to anyone, which is the state that sends the whole list — a `Store` built as a literal, which tests do, would otherwise have panicked on the first heartbeat.

Go: `weed/storage`, `weed/topology`, `weed/server/...` pass. Rust: 400 tests pass.

Refs #10603

  * Masters can request a complete volume list when needed.

items.title: s3: route object reads to the key's owner filer
items.body:
## Problem

S3 writes already route by key to the owner filer on the lock ring, where the entry is created. Reads, though, go to the gateway's local filer and treat its `NotFound` as authoritative (no failover on `NotFound`). So a `GET`/`HEAD` on one gateway can miss an object another gateway has just written, until the filers' `MetaAggregator` metadata replication catches up. This is the root cause behind the intermittent `404 NoSuchKey` in the `S3 Distributed Lock Regression Tests` job: the routed conditional `PUT` lands on the owner filer, but the read-back through the other gateway hits its local filer and races replication.

## Change

Resolve an object's entry from the key's **owner filer first** (the same route key the write path uses, so reader and writer agree on the owner), and fail over to the gateway's filer set **only on transport errors**.

- An owner `NotFound` stays authoritative: no fan-out across filers, and no resurrecting a peer's not-yet-replicated tombstone. A delete routed to the owner is visible immediately, and a genuine miss costs one lookup.
- Keys owned by the gateway's local filer are unchanged (the candidate list de-dups, so it's the current local fast path).
- A successful owner read does not move the gateway's sticky current filer (the owner is per-key, not a new default); a genuine failover still does.

`withFilerClientFailover` now takes a preferred start filer. The object-entry read fetchers (`fetchObjectEntry`, `fetchObjectEntryRequired` — covering `GET`, `HEAD`, `GetObjectAttributes`, ACL, and retention reads) pass the owner; every other caller passes `""` and keeps the existing current-filer behavior.

## Behavior during a cluster transition (ring churn)

The ring is versioned and monotonic — both the gateway's `LockClient.SetRing` and the master's `LockRing.SetSnapshot` reject stale/reordered updates. Before any ring arrives, `PrimaryForKey` returns `""` and reads fall back to plain local-first `getEntry`, so a starting gateway is unchanged.

- **Filer leaves / crashes:** a still-stale owner resolves to the dead filer → transport error → failover to a surviving filer (all carry eventually-consistent full copies). Availability preserved.
- **Stale ring / gateway version skew:** degrades to the eventual-consistency window reads already had; lock-path forwarding still guarantees exactly-one-winner for concurrent writes, so only read freshness softens.
- **Filer joins (ownership shifts to a not-yet-synced new owner):** the new owner can `NotFound` a just-moved key. To avoid a transient scale-up 404, the gateway `LockClient` now retains the previous ring for a cooling-off window (`PriorOwnerForKey`, mirroring the master's `LockRing.PriorOwner`); on the owner's `NotFound` it probes the key's **previous owner** once before treating the miss as final. Scoped to keys whose ownership actually moved and only within the window, so steady-state reads are untouched. This trades the transient 404 for a transient stale read if a delete routed to the new owner races the same window — the same authoritative-NotFound tradeoff, narrowed to the rebalance.

Invariant across all transitions: every filer a read can land on holds an eventually-consistent full copy, so the worst case is a transient, self-healing miss — never a hard failure, lost write, or stale-data-as-truth.

## Scope and trade-offs

- Single-object entry reads only. `LIST` spans many keys with different owners and can't be routed to one owner, so it stays eventually consistent.
- The shared `resolveObjectEntry` (used by write/delete preconditions, where the lock-path write lands on the local filer) is intentionally left local-first, so a precondition read can't diverge from where its write applies.
- Residual window: objects written through the non-routed lock path land on a gateway's local filer, so they can still read as absent on the owner until they replicate. This is the eventual-consistency tail shrunk to the minority of writes that bypass the owner.

## Testing

- `go test ./weed/s3api/` and `go test ./weed/cluster/...` pass; new `LockClient.PriorOwnerForKey` unit tests (move + expiry) cover the cooling-off window.
- `TestConditionalPutIfNoneMatchDistributedLockAcrossS3Gateways` (the previously flaky job) now passes deterministically — the cross-gateway read-back resolves on the owner without waiting for replication. Ran the cross-filer read path 5x with an immediate (non-retried) read; green every time. No test change was needed: the fix removes the race at its root.

items.title: s3: route metadata-only self-copy off the distributed lock
items.body:
Routes the metadata-only self-copy off the distributed lock — the last object-mutation path on the DLM. The fix is **serialization on the owner**, not optimistic concurrency.

> Builds on the merged routing foundation.

## What it is

A self-copy is `CopyObject` with source == destination + `x-amz-metadata-directive: REPLACE` — the standard way to update an object's metadata (user metadata, tags) in place without re-uploading the data. For a non-versioned bucket that's a **read-modify-write** of one entry, which is why it held the lock (a routed full-entry PUT from a gateway-side read would lose concurrent changes to other keys).

## What changes

The non-versioned in-place case routes as a `PATCH_EXTENDED` on the owner: the owner merges the new managed metadata onto a **fresh read under its per-path lock** (`set_extended` = the replacements, `delete_extended` = the managed keys the replace dropped) and bumps mtime. Because the merge happens on the owner under the lock, concurrent changes to non-managed keys (legal hold, retention, version id) are preserved rather than clobbered — no ETag/optimistic-concurrency needed.

`PATCH_EXTENDED` gains **`touch_mtime`** to bump `Attributes.Mtime`. Versioned/suspended self-copies create a new version (already routed via the copy finalize) and the no-owner bootstrap keep the lock.

items.title: filer: in-memory POSIX lock authority (Manager)
items.body:
Stacked on #9661 (codec) → #9660 (lock-set primitive).

The owner filer is the lock authority. Per the chosen design, lock state lives in **owner-filer memory** — not in replicated metadata — because advisory locks are transient coordination, not file data; keeping them off the meta-log avoids churn and doesn't pollute what subscribers see (the distributed lock manager holds its locks the same way).

This adds `posixlock.Manager`, the concurrent multi-inode layer over the per-inode `Set`:

- A `Set` per opaque inode `key` (the file's path, or `hl:<HardLinkId>` for a hardlinked inode, so all names of one inode share a `Set`).
- A `session → keys` index so reaping a dead mount's locks (`ReleaseSession`) is O(locks held), not a scan of every inode.
- `TryLock` / `Unlock` / `GetLk` / `ReleasePosixOwner` / `ReleaseFlockOwner` / `ReleaseSession`; empty sets and stale index entries are pruned on release. Mutex-guarded; safe for concurrent use.

The phase-2 codec is reused later to snapshot a `Set` for ownership-handoff/restart persistence — not per op.

Tests cover grant/conflict, key isolation, empty-key and index pruning (full and partial unlock), the flock/fcntl release split keeping the session indexed while the other namespace remains, cross-key session reaping, and a 16-goroutine whole-file flock churn under `-race` asserting mutual exclusion and that all maps drain to empty.

Still no callers — the routed `PosixLock` RPC that wraps this authority and the mount wiring come next.

items.title: fix(mount): don't strand a directory cached-but-empty when an eviction races a rebuild
items.body:
## Problem

A FUSE directory can end up flagged "fully cached" in `inodeToPath` while its entry store (metaCache leveldb) is empty. Once that happens, `lookupEntry` returns an authoritative `ENOENT` and `ReadDir` returns 0 entries without ever consulting the filer — so **every file in the directory vanishes from the mount even though the data is safe on the filer**. This is the intermittent `TestConcurrentFileOperations/ConcurrentReadWrite` FUSE flake (stat/ReadDir find nothing after writes that all succeeded), and it can hit any directory under enough concurrent create/lookup churn.

## Cause

The "complete" flag (`isChildrenCached`, in `inodeToPath`) and the cached entries (in the metaCache leveldb) live under two different locks. The hot-dir read-through path is safe because it runs in the metaCache apply loop, serialized with a build's `markCachedFn`. But three paths cleared the store **off** the apply loop, resetting the flag as a separate step:

- idle eviction (`loopEvictIdleDirCache`)
- kernel `Forget` → `onForgetDir` (runs after `Forget` releases its lock)
- the copy-range metadata fallback

A concurrent rebuild (`EnsureVisited` → `completeDirectoryBuild` → `MarkChildrenCached`) can publish a fresh, complete listing in the window between the flag reset and the `DeleteFolderChildren`. The stale wipe then deletes the freshly built entries, leaving the directory flagged cached over an empty store.

## Fix

Add `PurgeDirectoryChildren`, an apply-loop step that resets the cached flag (via a caller-supplied `resetFn`) and wipes the store together — serialized with `markCachedFn`, and skipped while the directory is building (an in-flight build owns the cache and will publish a complete listing). The three off-loop callers now route through it. The hot-dir path keeps calling `markDirectoryReadThrough` directly, since it already runs in the apply loop (enqueuing from there would deadlock).

Mount-only change. Added a regression test that pins the invariant: a purge that lands mid-build is skipped and the built cache survives.

* **Tests**

items.title: s3: route versioned COPY and delete-marker off the DLM
items.body:
Routes **versioned CopyObject** and **versioned delete-marker creation** off the distributed lock, reusing `FinalizeVersionedWrite` from the versioned-PutObject PR. No new filer op or proto.

> **Stacked PR** on the series (built on the MPU branch, which includes #9626–#9631). Merge after them.

## Why these fit

Both are the same shape as versioned PutObject — a **unique** version/marker file (`<obj>/.versions/<versionId>`, never collides) plus the **only contended mutation**, the latest-pointer flip (demote previous + set new) on the `.versions` directory entry. So both can serialize that flip on the `.versions` owner via `FinalizeVersionedWrite` (one local lock, precondition evaluated atomically) and drop the distributed lock.

## Change

- `finalizeCopyDestination` (VersioningEnabled) and `createDeleteMarker` gain an optional `owner` + `WriteCondition`. When the `.versions` owner is known they route the demote + pointer flip + precondition through `routedVersionedFinalize`, roll back the version/marker file if it fails, and return a precondition miss as `412`; otherwise they use the existing lock-based `updateLatestVersionInDirectory`.
- `CopyObjectHandler` and `DeleteObjectHandler` take the routed path for versioning-enabled destinations and skip `withObjectWriteLock`.

## Stays on the lock (deliberately)

Suspended versioning (multi-version `IsLatest` rewrite), version-specific deletes, the metadata-only self-copy, and the lifecycle delete-marker path. Each also falls back to the lock when the owner isn't known or the condition doesn't reduce to one primitive.

items.title: s3: route object-lock version-specific deletes off the distributed lock
items.body:
Routes **all** version-specific deletes off the distributed lock — real versions, the null version, object-lock WORM-checked versions, and governance-bypass. Closes the last design-level DLM boundary (only the no-owner bootstrap remains, by necessity).

> Builds on the merged routing foundation.

## Three primitives

- **`ObjectTransaction.condition_key`** — evaluate the condition against a named entry (the *version*) while the lock stays on `lock_key` (the *object*), so the WORM check targets the version but the pointer recompute serializes on the object.
- **`Recompute.exclude_name`** — omit a child from the scan, so the `.versions` pointer is repointed *before* the version blob is removed (a crash leaves a recoverable orphan, not a dangling pointer).
- **`WriteCondition.Clause.gate_key`/`gate_value`** — scope `IF_EXTENDED_TIME_ELAPSED` to a value of another extended key, so retention can be enforced only for `COMPLIANCE` mode. This is what lets governance bypass route: the filer reads the version's mode under the lock and decides, so the gateway never has to.

## What routes now

- **real version delete**: `[RECOMPUTE(exclude=version), DELETE version]` on the owner, locking the object.
- **null version delete**: direct `DELETE` of the regular object entry (no pointer to recompute).
- **object-lock**: legal hold (`IF_EXTENDED_NOT_EQUAL "ON"`) + retention (`IF_EXTENDED_TIME_ELAPSED`) gate the delete; a failed guard → `AccessDenied`.
- **governance bypass**: the retention guard is gated to `COMPLIANCE`, so governance-mode versions become deletable while compliance and legal hold still deny — no gateway-side read, no lock fallback.

Tests: `TestObjectTransactionVersionDeleteWithWorm` (condition_key + exclude_name) and `TestWriteConditionObjectLockGuards` bypass cases (compliance blocks, governance/unmoded allow).

items.title: s3: route single-entry object writes to the owner filer, off the DLM
items.body:
Takes the single-entry S3 object-write paths off the distributed lock and onto route-by-key + filer-local serialization, built on the filer primitives now on master.

> **Stacked on #9626** (lock-ring view + master broadcast to S3). Merge that first; the diff here is just the gateway routing delta.

## What changes

For **non-versioned, non-object-lock** buckets, `PutObject` and unversioned `DeleteObject` send their metadata mutation straight to the object key's **owner filer** (resolved from the lock-ring view) as a single-mutation `ObjectTransaction`. The owner serializes it with its local per-path lock and evaluates the precondition atomically, so these paths no longer acquire a distributed lock.

PUT and DELETE use the object's full path as the transaction lock key, so a concurrent create and delete of the same key serialize against each other on the owner.

Conditional headers reduce to `WriteCondition` clauses: `If-None-Match: *` -> `IF_NOT_EXISTS`, `If-Match: *` -> `IF_EXISTS`, and a single strong ETag -> `IF_ETAG_MATCH` / `IF_ETAG_NOT_MATCH`. A failed precondition comes back as a structured code and maps to the same `412` as today.

## Safe by construction

The fast path is opt-in per request and falls back to `withObjectWriteLock` for anything it does not fully cover:

- versioned or object-lock buckets
- preconditions that don't reduce to clauses: ETag lists, weak ETags, time-based, or combined `If-Match`+`If-None-Match`
- a post-create hook is present
- no owner in the ring view yet (`PrimaryForKey` returns empty until the ring arrives)
- the owner filer is unreachable (transport error -> fall back, not fail)
- a routed mutation error other than a failed precondition (the lock path re-runs and maps it exactly, and carries handling the raw mutation lacks, e.g. a directory marker that still has children)

## Handoff window (known limitation)

Correctness rests on all writers for a key routing to the same owner. On a stable ring they do. During a filer membership change there is a brief window where two gateways with skewed ring views could route the same key to two filers. Fully closing it needs an ownership-fencing barrier (follow-up).

## Scope

This covers the single-entry ops whose only object mutation is the final write — PUT and unversioned DELETE. Versioned writes, multipart completion, and copy route in later PRs in the series via `ObjectTransaction` (multi-entry) and stay on the lock until then.

## Tests

- `TestBuildWriteCondition` / `TestBuildDeleteCondition` — header to clause reduction, including every fall-back case.
- `TestSingleStrongETag` — strong vs weak/list ETag handling.
- `TestLockClientPrimaryForKey` — empty before the ring, owner after.

items.title: perf(filer): parallelize StreamMutateEntry with path-keyed scheduler
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes the ~500 QPS ceiling reported in #9138. The server-side handler for `StreamMutateEntry` processed one mutation at a time per stream (one goroutine per stream), capping a mount's aggregate metadata throughput at `1 / filer_store_service_time` regardless of client concurrency. On a real filer with typical 1–3 ms commit latency and 12 concurrent rclone processes, this showed as ~500 QPS.

Replace the serial loop with a per-request goroutine admitted by a path-keyed scheduler, adapted directly from filer.sync's `MetadataProcessor` (`weed/command/filer_sync_jobs.go`). Cross-path mutations run in parallel; same-path mutations serialize in arrival order; recursive delete and directory rename act as subtree barriers; directory attribute bumps stay non-barrier so they don't serialize file writes under them.

## Benchmark

2 ms simulated filer-store service delay, 12 client workers (matching the 12-rclone reproducer in #9138):

| handler | distinct paths | same path | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| serial (baseline) | 440 QPS | 441 QPS | 1/serviceDelay |
| semaphore only | 4902 QPS | 4907 QPS | **unsafe** — reorders same-path ops |
| **scheduler (this PR)** | **4934 QPS** | **439 QPS** | correct ordering |

The semaphore-only number shows the upper bound of raw parallelism. The scheduler matches it on distinct paths (the realistic 12-rclone case, ~11× lift) and correctly falls back to serial when the workload touches one path. Peak concurrent mutations at the handler equals client worker count on the distinct-path workload and pins to 1 on the same-path workload, as intended.

## Design (mirrors `MetadataProcessor`)

- Four conflict indexes per stream: `activeFilePaths`, `activeBarrierDirPaths`, `activeNonBarrierDirPaths`, `descendantCount`
- Same `pathConflicts` rules: barrier at p blocks anything at p or under p; same-path file+file blocks; incoming barrier waits for descendants; non-barrier dir (attr bump) never blocks descendants
- `cond.Wait` admission loop bounded by `streamMutateConcurrency = 64` per stream
- No timestamp heap / watermark (mutations aren't event-ordered like `SubscribeMetadata`)

Classification of `StreamMutateEntryRequest`:
- `Create` / `Update` → kind from `Entry.IsDirectory` (dir updates are non-barrier since `UpdateEntry` doesn't rename)
- `Delete` → barrier if `IsRecursive`, else file (target type not carried on the request)
- `Rename` → barrier on both `src` and `dst` paths

## Correctness and safety

- `syncStream` wrapper serializes `stream.Send` across worker goroutines (gRPC `Send` isn't concurrent-safe).
- Handler `wg.Wait()`s in-flight workers before returning on recv EOF/error so no worker writes to a torn-down stream.
- First fatal Send error from any worker propagates as the handler's return value, tearing the stream down.
- Per-stream goroutine cap (`64`) bounds resource use from a single noisy mount.

## Test plan

- [x] `go test -race ./weed/server/` — all scheduler/stream tests pass with race detector
- [x] `TestMutatePathAncestors` — ancestor walk
- [x] `TestClassifyMutation` — each request variant (create file/dir, update file/dir, delete recursive/not, rename)
- [x] `TestPathConflictSamePathFile` / `…BarrierBlocksSamePath` / `…BarrierBlocksDescendants` / `…IncomingBarrierWaitsForDescendants` / `…NonBarrierDirAllowsDescendants` / `…IncomingBarrierWaitsForSamePathNonBarrier`
- [x] `TestAdmitDoneLifecycle` — blocked admit unblocks on Done
- [x] `TestAdmitParallelDistinctPaths` — no self-blocking across paths
- [x] `TestAdmitConcurrencyCap` — cap enforced
- [x] `TestAdmitRenameTwoPathConflict` — rename holds both paths
- [x] `TestAdmitPressureFromManyWaiters` — 100-waiter smoke test, no lost wake-ups
- [x] `TestSchedulerOrderedParallelism` — end-to-end through real gRPC stack on both same-path and distinct-path workloads
- [x] Existing `TestReproStreamSerializationCeiling`, `TestServerSerialVsConcurrentHandler`, `TestStreamSyncVsAsyncClient`, and rename tests still pass
- [ ] Validate against real deployment in #9138 reproducer (12 rclone processes, 4.21 mount)

## Notes

`DeleteRequest` has no `IsDirectory`, so non-recursive deletes classify as `kindMutateFile`. This is safe: non-recursive delete of a directory fails at the store level if non-empty, and same-path serialization still orders the delete correctly against concurrent updates.

Related: #9138, #8770 (introduced the stream handler).

items.title: s3: serialize bucket config writes with field-level filer patches
items.body:
Fixes the lost-update race where concurrent `PutBucketVersioning` and `PutBucketEncryption` (e.g. from Terraform) each did a whole-entry read-modify-write of the bucket entry, so one silently overwrote the other's field with a stale copy.

> **Stacked on #9626** for `PrimaryForKey` + the lock-ring client. Merge that first.

## What changes

Each bucket-config write becomes a field-level `ObjectTransaction` on the bucket entry instead of a whole-entry rewrite:

- extended attributes (versioning, ownership, ACL, object-lock) -> `PATCH_EXTENDED` setting only the changed keys and deleting only the removed ones
- the metadata blob (tags, CORS, encryption) -> `set_content`, replacing only `Entry.content`

The transaction is routed to the bucket's owner filer (`PrimaryForKey`), and the filer merges the change onto a fresh read under that entry's per-path lock. Disjoint fields no longer clobber each other, and the two writers serialize on the same lock. The bucket-config cache is invalidated (not repopulated) after a patch, since the patched-away field may be stale in the cached copy.

`routableWriteOwner` no longer excludes object-lock buckets:
- a versioned PUT creates a new version (never overwrites a locked one), so it routes;

items.title: fix(s3/versioning): repair dangling latest-version pointer after partial delete
items.body:
## Background

While triaging a Veeam-against-SeaweedFS incident, the agent reported `Cloud.CreateCheckpoint` failures (`Storage … not found`, `immutability less than current storage immutability`). The first error traced back to a S3 `GET` on `…/Metadata/Lock/create.checkpoint/try` that returned `NoSuchKey`:

```
GetObject: Failed to get latest version for …/create.checkpoint/try:
stale latest-version pointer (file v_6755c8c09f6edc5bf64d87a6cbfea0dc)
could not self-heal: filer: no entry is found in filer store:
no remaining version in …/create.checkpoint/try.versions
```

The `.versions/` directory still had `ExtLatestVersionIdKey` / `ExtLatestVersionFileNameKey` set, but the version blob those names pointed at was gone from the filer. The read path's self-heal kicked in, scanned `.versions/`, found nothing valid, and returned `NoSuchKey` — which Veeam surfaced as a fatal storage error.

## Root cause

`deleteSpecificObjectVersion` in `weed/s3api/s3api_object_versioning.go` did two non-atomic filer operations:

```go
deleteErr := s3a.rm(versionsDir, versionFile, !metadataOnly, false)   // step 1
…
if isLatestVersion {
    err := s3a.updateLatestVersionAfterDeletion(bucket, normalizedObject)  // step 2
    if err != nil {
        glog.Warningf("…failed to update latest version after deletion: %v", err)
        // Don't return error since the deletion was successful
    }
}
```

Step 2 failures were swallowed — the client got `204 OK`, the pointer stayed pointing at a deleted blob. Step 2 fails for many ordinary reasons (filer briefly unreachable, gRPC timeout, lock contention, brief process pause), so at cluster scale the dangling-pointer population accumulates faster than the read-path heal can drain it. Every subsequent `GET` on a stranded key pays the 10-retry stale-pointer cost and returns `NoSuchKey`.

## Fix (three parts)

### 1. Pre-roll the pointer before the blob rm (`repointLatestBeforeDeletion`)
When we're about to delete the current latest, scan `.versions/` first to find the next-newest version *excluding* the one being deleted. Two cases:

- **Multi-version**: persist a pointer update to the prior latest, then rm the blob.
- **Singleton**: clear the pointer fields, then rm the blob.

A failure between the pointer update and the blob rm now leaves a recoverable orphan blob (pointer is already consistent — GETs succeed against the prior version, or correctly miss for singletons, without entering the 10-retry stale-pointer path).

### 2. Bounded retries + error propagation in `updateLatestVersionAfterDeletion`
All load-bearing filer ops (`list`, `getEntry`, `mkFile`, `rm`) are wrapped in `retryFilerOp` (6 attempts, exponential backoff, ≈6.3s worst case). When the budget is exhausted the function now returns a non-nil error.

`deleteSpecificObjectVersion` logs at `Error` level when the post-step fails and queues the path for the reconciler. The client still gets `204` (the blob rm itself succeeded; failing the request would make Veeam treat it as a hard storage error and retry the whole DELETE), but the inconsistency is no longer silent.

### 3. Background reconciler (`s3api_versioning_reconciler.go`)
A small in-memory queue + worker that drains stranded `.versions/` states without waiting for a client `GET`. Fed by failed `updateLatestVersionAfterDeletion` runs. Bounded queue (capacity 4096), capped retries (6 attempts), exponential backoff up to 30s, then gives up — the read-path heal remains as a last-resort safety net.

## Tests

`weed/s3api/s3api_versioning_reconciler_test.go` covers:
- Queue dedup on enqueue
- Capacity clamp behaviour
- `popReady` only releases due candidates
- Requeue with backoff
- Give-up after `versionsHealMaxRetries`
- `retryFilerOp` success-before-exhaustion and propagate-after-exhaustion

Existing `s3api_object_versioning_self_heal_test.go` tests still pass.

## Test plan

- [x] `go test ./weed/s3api/... -count=1` — all green locally
- [x] `go build ./...` — clean
- [ ] Verify against a busy versioning workload (Veeam or s3-tests `test_versioning_*`) that the `NoSuchKey on freshly-PUT lock` symptom no longer reproduces and that no new logs surface from the reconciler under healthy operation

items.title: s3: commit a versioned PutObject and its latest pointer in one transaction
items.body:
A versioned PutObject wrote the version file and flipped the `.versions` latest pointer in two separate routed transactions, leaving a window where a crash could land the version with a stale pointer.

Fold the `RECOMPUTE_LATEST` into the version file's `PUT` so both commit atomically under the object's per-path lock. The recompute, applied after the `PUT` in the same transaction, scans `.versions/` and sees the new version, then flips the pointer and demotes the prior latest. This matches the delete path, which already recomputes and deletes in one transaction.

`putToFiler` now takes a `putFinalize` describing the finalize step: routed mutations folded into the `PUT`, or an `afterCreate` run under the object write lock when there's no ring owner. Suspended versioning keeps its `afterCreate`-only form.

Off the ring (no `objectWriteLockClient`), behavior is unchanged: `CreateEntry` then `updateLatestVersionInDirectory` under the lock.

Multipart-complete, copy-to-versioned, and delete-marker finalizes still use the separate `routedVersionedFinalize` (they also write their blob via `mkFile` rather than routing it); converting those is a larger follow-up.
